title: Replace conditional with polymorphism
summary: Turn type-checking switches into objects that know their own behaviour, one safe step at a time.

steps.title: The repeated switch
body: decimal Fee(Account a) => a.Type switch { "basic" => 0, "plus" => 5, "pro" => 12, _ => throw ... };
int FreeTransfers(Account a) => a.Type switch { "basic" => 3, "plus" => 10, "pro" => 100, _ => throw ... };
string Badge(Account a) => a.Type switch { "basic" => "", "plus" => "+", "pro" => "PRO", _ => throw ... };
Three switches on the same type code. Adding `"student"` is shotgun surgery: three edits, and the compiler will not tell you if you miss one.

steps.prompt: Which smell does this code show most clearly?
code: decimal Fee(Account a) => a.Type switch { "basic" => 0, "plus" => 5, "pro" => 12, _ => throw ... };
int FreeTransfers(Account a) => a.Type switch { "basic" => 3, "plus" => 10, "pro" => 100, _ => throw ... };
string Badge(Account a) => a.Type switch { "basic" => "", "plus" => "+", "pro" => "PRO", _ => throw ... };
options: Repeated switch on a type code, leading to shotgun surgery

steps.title: The refactoring, in steps
body: 1. Create an interface (or abstract class) with one member per switch: `IPlan { decimal Fee; int FreeTransfers; string Badge; }`.
2. Create one class per case, copying each switch arm into it.
3. Give `Account` an `IPlan` instead of a string; replace each switch with a call (`a.Plan.Fee`). Run the tests after each.
4. Keep **one** switch where outside input (`"pro"` from a database) becomes an object: the factory.
interface IPlan { decimal Fee { get; } int FreeTransfers { get; } string Badge { get; } }
class Basic : IPlan { public decimal Fee => 0; public int FreeTransfers => 3; public string Badge => ""; }
Adding `Student` is now one class plus one factory line.

steps.prompt: Arrange the steps of Replace Conditional with Polymorphism in a safe order.
lines: Write tests for the current behaviour of every switch
Create the interface with one member per switch
Replace each switch with a call through the interface, testing after each
Keep a single factory switch at the input edge

code: IPlan[] plans = { new Basic(), new Pro() };
interface IPlan { decimal Fee { get; } string Badge { get; } }
class Basic : IPlan { public decimal Fee => 0; public string Badge => "b"; }
class Pro : IPlan { public decimal Fee => 12; public string Badge => "PRO"; }

steps.title: Replace the switches
prompt: Refactor the three switches into polymorphism:
- `interface IPlan { decimal Fee { get; } int FreeTransfers { get; } string Badge { get; } }`
- classes `Basic`, `Plus`, `Pro` with the values from the switches
- `static class Plans` with `static IPlan From(string code)`, the only switch left, throwing `ArgumentException` for unknown codes
starter: decimal Fee(string type) => type switch { "basic" => 0m, "plus" => 5m, "pro" => 12m, _ => throw new ArgumentException(type) };
int FreeTransfers(string type) => type switch { "basic" => 3, "plus" => 10, "pro" => 100, _ => throw new ArgumentException(type) };
string Badge(string type) => type switch { "basic" => "", "plus" => "+", "pro" => "PRO", _ => throw new ArgumentException(type) };
solution: class Basic : IPlan { public decimal Fee => 0m; public int FreeTransfers => 3; public string Badge => ""; }
class Plus : IPlan { public decimal Fee => 5m; public int FreeTransfers => 10; public string Badge => "+"; }
class Pro : IPlan { public decimal Fee => 12m; public int FreeTransfers => 100; public string Badge => "PRO"; }
public static IPlan From(string code) => code switch
template: Dojo.Eq("all three plans", new List<string> { "0/3/", "5/10/+", "12/100/PRO" }, dojoSummary);
Dojo.Check("pro is a Pro", Plans.From("pro") is Pro, "From(\"pro\") should return a Pro");

require.message: Exactly one switch is left (in the factory)
